steps.title: South of Burgundy
steps.body: Beaujolais lies just south of the Mâconnais, north of Lyon, in eastern France. It has about 13,000 hectares of vines on rolling hills. The climate is semi-continental, warmer than the Côte d'Or. Administratively it belongs to Burgundy, but its grape, soils and style are its own.

steps.title: North and south
steps.body: Beaujolais divides in two. The north, the Haut-Beaujolais, has pink granite and schist hills, where the best wines grow: Beaujolais-Villages and the ten crus. The south, the Bas-Beaujolais, has clay and limestone, called pierres dorées, golden stones, and makes simpler Beaujolais, including much of the Nouveau.

steps.prompt: Where do Beaujolais' best wines grow?
steps.explanation: Granite in the north suits Gamay best.

steps.title: Lyon's wine
steps.body: Beaujolais has long been the everyday wine of Lyon, France's food capital, served in its bouchons, traditional bistros, from a pot, a thick-bottomed bottle. The saying goes that Lyon is watered by three rivers: the Rhône, the Saône and the Beaujolais.

steps.prompt: Beaujolais' northern hills are mainly granite.
steps.explanation: Yes. Pink granite and schist dominate the north.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Beaujolais lies between the Mâconnais and Lyon
Northern granite gives the best wines; the south is limestone
